entries.meaning: A cavalry command turned playful rallying cry. Americans use it to launch a group into motion — a game, a chore, a run to the car — with a deliberate whiff of the battlefield about it, and it is the four-note fanfare every stadium organ plays.
examples: "Charge!" he yelled, and forty second-graders ran for the playground.
Everybody grab a box off the truck. Charge!
The organ played the little fanfare and the whole ballpark yelled charge.
Charge! Last one to the water buys lunch.
She raised her coffee cup like a sword and said, "Charge."
entries.русский: вперёд! / в атаку! — шутливый боевой клич, поднимающий компанию с места
entries.see also: come on, let's go, go get 'em

entries.meaning: The workhorse of American encouragement: it urges someone to hurry, to follow, or to keep trying, and it is what fans shout at a struggling team. Said flat with a falling tone it flips into protest or disbelief — oh, come on means you cannot be serious — so tone does all the work.
examples: Come on, we're going to miss the previews.
"C'mon, c'mon, c'mon," he muttered, watching the free throw.
Come on, buddy, you've got one more lap in you.
Come on over — the grill's already hot.
Oh, come on, that was clearly a foul.
Come on now, you know I'd never say that about you.
entries.русский: давай! / ну же! — подгоняет и подбадривает; ровным тоном — «да ладно тебе»
entries.see also: let's go, go on, keep going

entries.meaning: A locker-room and job-site push meaning go do the work, hard, starting now. Coaches, trainers, and foremen use it constantly; in an office it sounds like you are quoting a coach on purpose.
examples: All right, boys — get after it.
Weights are racked and the clock's running. Get after it.
He clapped once, said "get after it," and the whole team hit the field.
You've got four hours and a full truck to unload. Get after it.
Get after it today, because tomorrow's forecast is ugly.
entries.русский: за дело! / вперёд, вкалывай — очень разг., из спортзала и со стройки
entries.see also: let's get it, go get 'em, charge

entries.meaning: The command that tells a horse to start moving, borrowed for people. Off a horse it is jokey — a way to say let's move that makes the speaker sound like a cowboy on purpose.
examples: Giddyup! she said, and the pony started down the trail.
Coats on, shoes on, giddyup — the bus is at the corner.
He signed the last page, slapped the folder shut, and said, "Giddyup."
Giddy-up, little man. Bath time.
The light turned green and the guy behind us leaned out and hollered, "Giddyup!"
entries.русский: но! / пошёл! — окрик лошади; о людях шутливое «поехали, шевелись»
entries.see also: let's go, come on, yee-haw

entries.meaning: Permission and encouragement in one: take the chance, I'm behind you. It answers a hesitation, and on fourth down it is what the whole stadium yells at the coach.
examples: If you want to apply, go for it — worst case they say no.
"Can I have the last slice?" "Go for it."
Fourth and one on the forty. Go for it!
She's been talking about that tattoo for a year, so I told her to go for it.
Go for it, man. You'll regret not trying a lot more than you'll regret failing.
entries.русский: дерзай! / давай, пробуй — разрешение и поддержка разом
entries.see also: have at it, you got this, go get 'em

entries.meaning: A send-off for someone walking into a contest, an interview, or a stage. It casts whatever they are about to face as an opponent, which is exactly why it lands as a boost.
examples: Straighten your tie. Go get 'em.
"Go get 'em, tiger," his mom said, and shut the car door.
She's got the closing argument this morning — go get 'em.
Get 'em, Rosie! Two more points!
He texted one line before the audition: "Go get 'em."
entries.русский: покажи им! / задай им — напутствие идущему на испытание
entries.variants: get 'em, go get 'em, tiger, go git 'em
entries.see also: knock 'em dead, break a leg, sic 'em

entries.meaning: Two jobs: it invites a speaker to keep talking, and it nudges a hesitating person to go ahead and act. Said with a smile and a wave of the hand it also works as mock-modest deflection — oh, go on means you're flattering me, keep going.
examples: Go on — I want to hear what she said next.
Go on, ask her. She's not going to bite.
"You should hear him play." "Oh, go on."
He stopped talking, and the detective just nodded and said, "Go on."
Go on, take the last one. Nobody else is going to eat it.
entries.русский: продолжай; ну давай же — приглашение говорить дальше или решиться
entries.see also: keep going, come on, there you go

entries.meaning: Cheerful permission to go ahead and start — usually with something the speaker is handing over: a plate of food, a broken appliance, a fight they are staying out of. It grants the floor rather than praising anything.
examples: Tools are in the garage. Have at it.
"Mind if I take a crack at the crossword?" "Have at it."
There's a whole tray of leftovers in the fridge — have at it.
He pushed the keyboard across the desk and said, "Have at it."
If you two want to argue about the thermostat all night, have at it.
entries.русский: валяй! / приступай — разг. разрешение начать: «дело твоё»
entries.variants: have at 'em, have at thee (jocular, archaic)
entries.see also: go for it, go on, charge

entries.meaning: The psych-up said at the threshold: everybody is assembled, the thing is about to start, and this is the sentence that starts it. Unlike let's go, it never means leave — it points at one specific job both speakers already have in mind, which is why it works just as well muttered to yourself as shouted at a group.
examples: Gloves on, bags out. Let's do this.
"Let's do this," she told the mirror, and walked out to the podium.
Four people, one couch, three flights of stairs — let's do this.
The anesthesiologist asked if she had any questions. "Nope. Let's do it."
"We could keep talking about it for another month." "No. Let's do this."
entries.русский: ну, приступим! / поехали — настрой перед конкретным делом, не «пойдём»
entries.variants: let's do it, all right, let's do this
entries.see also: let's go, let's get it, here we go

entries.meaning: A hype phrase out of sports and hip-hop meaning let's start, and let's dominate. It lives in locker rooms and group chats; in a staff meeting it reads as trying too hard.
examples: Bags are packed, van's loaded. Let's get it.
He posted a picture of the empty field with the caption "Let's get it."
First day of camp — let's get it, fellas.
"You ready?" "Let's get it."
Let's get it, we're only down six with a whole half to play.
entries.русский: погнали! / вперёд, порвём — очень разг., из спорта и хип-хопа
entries.variants: let's get it in, let's gettit
entries.see also: let's go, get after it, boom

entries.meaning: Literally an invitation to leave, but shouted after a big play or good news it means yes — that is exactly what I wanted. The lengthened spelling let's gooo is how the celebratory sense gets written online, because the plain spelling looks like you are just telling somebody to get in the car.
examples: Let's go! He made the putt!
Grab your jacket, let's go.
"We got the apartment." "LET'S GO."
Three seconds left and we're up one — let's go, defense!
She read the acceptance email twice and whispered, "Let's goooo."
entries.русский: пошли!; а также «даёшь!» — торжествующий возглас после удачи
entries.see also: let's get it, come on, go

entries.meaning: A literary keep moving forward, used to close a speech, an email, or a bad day. It concedes that the setback happened and announces that the group is proceeding anyway.
examples: The quarter was rough, but the pipeline looks strong. Onward.
She ended every newsletter the same way: "Onward and upward."
Well, that meeting was a disaster. Onward.
Onward, friends — there's a lot of work ahead and not much daylight.
He signed the note "Onward," which was as sentimental as he ever got.
entries.русский: вперёд! / идём дальше — книжн., подводит черту под неудачей
entries.see also: keep going, chin up, charge

entries.meaning: The command that sets a dog on a target, used with people as rowdy encouragement to go after an opponent, an argument, or a rival team. It is aggressive by design — friendly among fans and friends, hostile anywhere it could be taken literally.
examples: The mailman came up the walk and Grandpa laughed and said, "Sic 'em, Duke."
She's about to cross-examine the witness. Sic 'em.
"Sic 'em, Bears!" is the entire chant at Baylor.
He rolled up his sleeves and I said, "Sic 'em, tiger."
Somebody finally posted the receipts in the comments — sic 'em.
entries.русский: фас! — очень разг., натравить собаку или человека на противника
entries.see also: go get 'em, give 'em hell, charge

entries.meaning: The shout of approval at the end of a performance. The Italian gender endings survive in opera houses — brava for a soprano, bravi for the whole cast — but most Americans use bravo for everybody, and away from a stage it is often faintly sarcastic.
examples: The aria ended and half the balcony was on its feet yelling bravo.
Brava! She held that last note forever.
Bravo to whoever finally fixed the printer.
He read the closing paragraph out loud and said, "Bravo. That's the piece."
"I ate the entire pizza by myself." "Bravo."
entries.русский: браво! — возглас одобрения после выступления
entries.variants: brava (to a woman), bravi (to a group), bravo!!!
entries.see also: encore, hear hear, well done

entries.meaning: Raised-glass approval. As a toast it salutes whoever is named; in three cheers for Dana it introduces an actual organized cheer; and cheers used alone as a sign-off or a casual thanks is British, which Americans notice immediately.
examples: Cheers — to twenty-five years and counting.
Eight glasses came up over the middle of the table and everybody said cheers at slightly different times.
Three cheers for the groundskeepers! Hip hip —
She lifted her glass and said, "Cheers. You did it."
My coworker in London ends every email with "Cheers," and it still reads as foreign to me.
entries.русский: за здоровье! / ваше здоровье — тост; одиночное cheers как «спасибо, пока» — британское
entries.see also: hip hip hooray, hooray, hear hear

entries.meaning: The shout that demands one more song. Americans chant it as much as they mean it as a request, and off the stage it survives as a joking do that again.
examples: The house lights stayed down and the crowd started chanting "Encore! Encore!"
Encore! Play the one about the river!
He nailed the impression and his sisters all yelled encore.
Encore, Dad! Do the coin thing again.
"Encore!" my grandmother called, clapping over her head, and the pianist sat back down.
entries.русский: бис! — требование исполнить ещё раз
entries.see also: bravo, take a bow, hooray

entries.meaning: The emcee's call for applause, always followed by the name of whoever is walking out or being honored. It is an instruction to the room rather than a compliment to the person — the praise is the noise it produces — and away from a microphone it works as mock fanfare for something ordinary.
examples: Give it up for the band. They drove nine hours to be here.
"Let's hear it for the graduating class!"
Give it up for Marcus, everybody — twenty years on this crew.
He came back through the door with the pizzas and somebody yelled, "Give it up for the delivery guy."
Put your hands together for our next reader.
entries.русский: поприветствуем (такого-то)! / аплодисменты — ! — призыв конферансье хлопать
entries.variants: let's hear it for —, put your hands together for —, round of applause for —
entries.see also: encore, take a bow, bravo

entries.meaning: The bare stadium cheer, almost always followed by the name of the team or person you are backing. Repeated fast — go go go — it stops being encouragement and becomes urgency, the word you shout at somebody who has to move right now.
examples: Go, Wildcats!
Go, Maya! You're almost at the finish line!
"Go go go!" the coach yelled as the runner took the baton.
He forwarded the mandatory-fun email to me with two words on top: "Go, team."
Go, Dad — you've got this hill.
entries.русский: вперёд, наши! — кричалка с именем команды; go go go — «давай-давай, быстрее!»
entries.see also: let's go, come on, you got this

entries.meaning: Two things at once: the stadium chant that carries a team through a drive — here we go, Steelers, here we go — and the breath somebody takes alone, out loud, right before starting the hard thing. Add one word and it inverts: here we go again is weariness, and everybody hears the difference.
examples: Here we go, Steelers, here we go!
Seat belts on, coffee in the holder. Here we go.
The house lights went down and she whispered, "Here we go."
Here we go — third and goal from the two.
His mother started in about the wedding again, and my husband muttered, "Here we go."
entries.русский: ну, начали! / поехали — перед стартом; here we go again — «опять двадцать пять»
entries.variants: here we go now, here we go again (resigned, not a cheer)
entries.see also: let's go, let's do this, go

entries.meaning: A call-and-response cheer: one person shouts hip hip and everybody else answers hooray, traditionally three times. It is now mostly a birthday-party and retirement-party thing, and among adults it is a little corny on purpose.
examples: Hip hip — "Hooray!"
Let's hear it for the birthday girl: hip hip hooray!
The whole office did an awkward hip hip hooray around the sheet cake.
"Hip hip hooray!" the campers shouted three times, exactly as instructed.
Thirty years at the same company — hip hip hooray, and somebody hand him the plaque.
entries.русский: гип-гип — ура! — кричалка «запевала и хор», обычно трижды
entries.see also: hooray, huzzah, cheers

entries.meaning: The U.S. Army's all-purpose shout of agreement, readiness, and morale — roughly understood, and I'm fired up about it. It is branch-specific: Marines say oorah, sailors and Coast Guardsmen say hooyah, and mixing them up is the kind of mistake veterans catch instantly.
examples: "Everybody clear on the timeline?" "Hooah, Sergeant."
Hooah! Let's move.
He answered every question that morning with a flat hooah.
The general finished his remarks and four hundred soldiers answered hooah.
"Chow's in ten." "Hooah."
entries.русский: так точно! / есть! — боевой возглас армии США (только сухопутные войска)
entries.see also: oorah, rah, charge

entries.meaning: The standard English shout of joy and approval. Hooray and hurray are the everyday spellings; hurrah is older and more literary, and it sounds like a history book or a sea story.
examples: Hooray! The power's back on.
Everyone yelled hooray when the principal announced the snow day.
Hurray for whoever brought donuts.
"Hurrah!" the crew shouted as the sails filled.
Well, hooray — the plumber says it's only the flapper valve.
entries.русский: ура! — общий возглас радости и одобрения
entries.see also: hip hip hooray, huzzah, yay

entries.meaning: The Navy and Coast Guard answer to the Army's hooah — acknowledgment, readiness, and morale in two syllables, loudest in SEAL and rescue-swimmer training, where it is shouted back at an instructor dozens of times a day. The three service shouts are not interchangeable: hooah is Army, oorah is Marine Corps, hooyah is Navy and Coast Guard, and using the wrong one is the giveaway that a movie had no veterans on set.
examples: "Do you understand the standard?" "Hooyah, Instructor!"
The whole boat crew answered hooyah and picked the log back up.
Hooyah — surf zone in five minutes.
Twenty-six years in the Navy, and he still answers the phone on his birthday with a hooyah.
She finished the swim, coughed up half the Pacific, and got out one hooyah.
entries.русский: ура! / есть! — возглас ВМС и Береговой охраны США, не путать с hooah и oorah
entries.see also: hooah, oorah, rah

entries.meaning: An antique hooray, alive today mainly at Renaissance fairs, in historical fiction, and in the mouths of people being theatrically pleased. Nobody says it plainly anymore.
examples: Huzzah! The turkey leg cart has been located.
The whole tavern stood up and shouted huzzah three times.
She got the last spot in the garage and yelled, "Huzzah!"
Huzzah — the build finally passed.
"Huzzah," he said flatly, holding up the new stapler.
entries.русский: ура! — устар., ныне только шутливо или на исторических фестивалях
entries.see also: hooray, bravo, yay

entries.meaning: A Spanish shout of approval, borrowed whole and never translated. In bullfighting and flamenco it marks the exact instant of a clean pass or a hard turn, and it reached most Americans through soccer, where olé, olé, olé is what a crowd sings when its team is stringing passes together and running out the clock. Written without the accent it looks like the Scandinavian name Ole, which is why the accent tends to survive even in casual typing.
examples: The cape came around and half the plaza shouted olé.
The dancer's heels hit the last beat and somebody in the front row called out olé.
Four minutes left, up two goals, and the whole away end started in with "Olé! Olé! Olé!"
He got the car into that spot on the first try and his sister said, "Olé."
The waiter set down the paella, lifted the empty pan over his head, and the table gave him an olé.
entries.русский: оле! — исп. возглас одобрения: коррида, фламенко, футбольные трибуны
entries.see also: bravo, hooray, yeah

entries.meaning: The U.S. Marine Corps shout — agreement, enthusiasm, and identity in two syllables. Like hooah, it belongs to one branch, and Marines use it with each other far more than they use it with civilians.
examples: "Feeling motivated this morning?" "Oorah, Staff Sergeant."
Oorah! Semper Fi.
The recruiter grinned, shook my hand, and said, "Oorah."
Every birthday text from his old platoon just said "Oorah."
He finished the story with a quiet oorah and left it there.
entries.русский: ура! / есть! — боевой возглас морской пехоты США
entries.see also: hooah, rah, charge

entries.meaning: The bare syllable of an old cheerleading chant. Doubled as rah-rah it usually describes enthusiasm instead of expressing it — a rah-rah speech is one that is all energy and no content.
examples: Rah! Rah! Go, Panthers!
The squad came onto the track chanting "Rah, rah, sis boom bah."
Rah, team. That's about all the enthusiasm I have left today.
Somebody in the back yelled rah and got exactly nobody to join in.
"Rah!" she said, pumping her fist about two inches.
entries.русский: ура! — слог старой кричалки болельщиков; rah-rah — «шумно, но пусто»
entries.variants: rah rah, rah-rah-rah, sis boom bah
entries.see also: hooah, oorah, go

entries.ipa: Not speech, and no phonemic transcription of it is honest. It is a tone, not a syllable: air forced through pursed lips, or through two fingers hooked back against the tongue, at a pitch high enough to cut through a crowd. The cheering pattern is one long shriek or a run of short rising blasts. In writing it is described (he whistled) rather than spelled, though comics use wheet and fweet.
entries.meaning: The loudest applause one person can produce without help, and in an American crowd it means straightforward approval — it goes up at concerts, graduations, rodeos, and school assemblies, always stacked on top of clapping rather than instead of it. Two things set it apart from everything else in this category. It has no agreed spelling, because it has no speech sounds in it. And one specific pattern, the two-note falling wolf whistle aimed at a person's body, is not encouragement in any current American reading: it is street harassment, it is heard that way regardless of what the whistler intended, and the friendly crowd whistle does not protect it.
examples: Her name was called and her whole row stood up and whistled.
Somebody two seats back put two fingers in his mouth and let out a whistle that made my ear ring.
The band came back out for the encore and the whistling went on for a solid minute.
He whistled through his teeth when the tow truck finally pulled the pickup out of the ditch.
"Don't whistle at people," her mother said. "Clap, like a human being."
entries.русский: свист — одобрительный свист в толпе; «волчий свист» вслед человеку — уже приставание
entries.see also: whoop, give it up for, woo-hoo

entries.meaning: A loud, wordless holler of excitement, spelled out. Doubled as whoop whoop it works as a written cheer, and because it also imitates a siren it shows up in songs and jokes about police.
examples: Whoop! That's my kid up on that stage.
Whoop whoop! Friday at last.
"Whoop!" he yelled, and threw his cap in the air.
Whoop whoop — pizza's here, everybody.
She read the score off her phone and let out a whoop that startled the dog.
entries.русский: у-ух! / гиканье — громкий бессловесный вопль восторга
entries.see also: woo-hoo, yee-haw, yay

entries.meaning: The standard American whoop of delight, said as often as it is shouted. Clipped to woo it is what people yell from an audience; stretched out in writing it is pure excitement with the volume left in. Said perfectly flat, it is one of the most reliable sarcasm markers in the language.
examples: Woo-hoo! No school tomorrow!
"Woo!" somebody yelled from the back of the bar.
We got the loan — woohoo!
She typed "wooooo" in the group chat and then about twelve exclamation points.
He said "woo-hoo" in the flattest voice imaginable when they announced the mandatory training.
entries.русский: у-ху! / ура — стандартный американский вопль радости; ровным тоном — сарказм
entries.see also: whoop, yay, woot

entries.meaning: A written cheer out of early-2000s gaming chat, spelled with zeros in its heyday. It still turns up in group chats and commit messages, where it now reads as either affectionate or slightly dated.
examples: Woot! Build's green.
"Tickets are in my cart." "w00t"
Woot woot — first weekend off since March.
She replied to the entire thread with a single "woot."
Got the last two seats on the aisle. Woot.
entries.русский: ура! / йес — интернет-сленг нулевых, писался w00t
entries.see also: woo-hoo, yay, yas

entries.meaning: An emphatic, drawn-out yes used to hype somebody up — approval with a lot of energy behind it. It is shouted out loud at least as often as it is typed, so calling it an internet word undersells it. It comes out of Black and Latino ballroom culture and spread through drag performance and social media, and it stays heavily marked: in a straight white mouth, or in a work channel, it reads as an impression of somebody else's speech rather than as enthusiasm.
examples: Yas! That dress is unbelievable on you.
"I quit this morning." "YAAAS. Finally."
She commented "yas queen" on every single photo.
Yasss, book the trip. Do it.
The whole chat went yas when the tour dates dropped.
entries.русский: да-а-а! — очень разг., восторженное «да» из ballroom-культуры; в чужих устах звучит как пародия
entries.see also: yes, yay, woo-hoo

entries.meaning: The small, warm cheer — happiness at good news rather than triumph over anybody. It is gentle enough for a text to a friend and extremely common in speech to and from children, which is why a shouted yay from a grown man usually reads as a joke.
examples: Yay! You made it.
"The results came back clean." "Yay!"
Yay, cake.
She texted back "yayyy" and about six exclamation points.
Yay for whoever finally fixed the coffee machine.
entries.русский: ура! — тихая тёплая радость, часто в речи с детьми
entries.see also: hooray, woo-hoo, yes

entries.meaning: Shouted rather than spoken, yeah stops being agreement and becomes a cheer — the noise a crowd makes when the band starts the song everybody came for. Drawn out, it also works as loud approval of somebody else's decision.
examples: Yeah! That's what I'm talking about!
The first chord hit and ten thousand people yelled yeah.
"I told him no." "Yeahhh. Good."
Yeah, buddy! Look at that catch!
She jumped off the last rock, landed clean, and shouted "Yeah!"
entries.русский: да-а! / е-е! — не согласие, а выкрик восторга толпы
entries.see also: yes, whoop, let's go

entries.meaning: The cowboy holler of delight. Ranch country still uses it straight; everywhere else it is playful — a way of saying this is great while doing a Western accent.
examples: Yee-haw! We're going to Texas.
He hit the jump, landed it, and let out a yee-haw.
"Boots are two-for-one this week." "Yeehaw."
Yee-haw, everybody — the barn dance starts at seven.
The rider made all eight seconds and the whole arena went yee-haw.
entries.русский: и-ха! / эге-гей! — ковбойский вопль восторга, вне ранчо шутливо
entries.see also: whoop, giddyup, woo-hoo

entries.meaning: Said sharply with a fist pump, yes is not an answer to anything — it is the sound of a win landing. It is the most common American exclamation of triumph, and in writing the extra s's carry the volume.
examples: Yes! I got the job!
"YES!" he screamed at the television.
The ball dropped in and she just said, quietly, "Yes."
Yesss, they're bringing back the breakfast menu.
He read the text, closed his eyes, and whispered yes.
entries.русский: да! / есть! — возглас торжества, а не ответ на вопрос
entries.see also: boom, let's go, yeah

entries.meaning: A worn-down that's the boy — quick praise delivered in the moment rather than afterward. It is affectionate but hierarchical: it fits a coach to a player, a handler to a dog, an older person to a younger one, and between equals it can land as condescending, especially attagirl said to a grown woman.
examples: Attaboy! That's how you block.
"Atta girl," her father said as she backed the trailer into the driveway.
He scratched the dog's ears and said, "Attaboy, Cooper."
Attaway, Marcus — right down the middle.
She landed the account, and all he said was "attagirl," which somehow made it worse.
entries.русский: молодец! / вот так! — похвала сверху вниз (тренер, хозяин собаке); attagirl — «молодчина»
entries.variants: atta boy, attagirl, atta girl, attaway, that-a-boy
entries.see also: good job, way to go, nice work

entries.meaning: The sound of an explosion used to punctuate a success, usually your own. It marks the exact moment something lands: the shot goes in, the code compiles, the argument ends.
examples: Two clicks, one password reset, and boom — you're back in.
Boom! Nothing but net.
He flipped the last card over. "Boom. Full house."
You put the pan in at 400 for twenty minutes and boom, dinner.
She dropped the last folder on his desk. Boom. A day early.
entries.русский: бам! / вот так! — очень разг., звук взрыва как точка в собственном успехе
entries.variants: boom!, boom goes the dynamite, boom shakalaka
entries.see also: nailed it, there you go, yes

entries.meaning: The plainest praise in American English, safe in every setting. It is also the default thing adults say to small children, so between adult peers it can sound faintly like a gold star — nice work is the safer version at the office.
examples: Good job, everybody. That was a clean launch.
"Good job!" the coach called as she came off the field.
Great job on the deck — it looks brand new.
He studied the drawing for a long moment and said, "Good job, bud."
Nice job getting all of that done before the holiday.
entries.русский: молодец / хорошая работа — простейшая похвала, детям звучит уместнее, чем коллегам
entries.variants: great job, nice job, good job!
entries.see also: nice work, well done, way to go

entries.meaning: Public credit where credit is due, from the old gesture of removing your hat in respect. It is slightly formal and shows up most in speeches, toasts, and thank-you notes.
examples: Hats off to the volunteers who ran registration all weekend.
My hat's off to you — I could not have kept my temper like that.
Hats off to the kitchen. That was the best meal we've had all year.
He raised his glass and said, "Hats off to thirty years of this nonsense."
Hats off, honestly. You made a hard thing look easy.
entries.русский: снимаю шляпу — публичное признание чужой заслуги
entries.variants: hats off to —, my hat's off to you
entries.see also: kudos, props, well done

entries.meaning: A shout of agreement with something just said, out of parliamentary practice, where members could not applaud and so called out hear him. Americans use it at toasts, board meetings, and dinner-table speeches, and the spelling here here is wrong in a way people notice.
examples: "Hear, hear!" someone called from the end of the table.
He quoted the whole paragraph into the group chat and added, "Hear, hear."
He finished the toast and half the room said hear hear.
"Nobody should have to work two jobs to make rent." "Hear, hear."
Hear hear to that, and to the people who did the actual work.
entries.русский: верно! / поддерживаю! — книжн., возглас согласия с оратором или тостом
entries.see also: bravo, cheers, well done

entries.meaning: Credit and praise, from a Greek word for glory. It is a singular noun that looks plural, so careful writers avoid a kudo; in practice Americans use it as a ready-made compliment, especially in work email and internal announcements.
examples: Kudos to the whole team for turning that around in two days.
Kudos — that was a genuinely hard call and you made it.
She sent a company-wide kudos to the night shift.
Kudos to Ellen for catching the error before it went to print.
The review gave kudos to the lighting designer and barely mentioned the cast.
entries.русский: респект / честь и хвала — похвала, особенно в рабочей переписке
entries.see also: props, hats off, good job

entries.meaning: Approval of somebody else's choice, especially one you would not make yourself. Meant sincerely it is generous; delivered with a shrug it means that's your business, not mine, which is how it usually lands when the choice sounds unwise.
examples: She's moving to Alaska to fly bush planes. More power to her.
If you can eat like that and still run marathons, more power to you.
"I'm doing the whole remodel without a contractor." "More power to you."
More power to 'em — somebody has to be willing to do that job.
He wants to try stand-up at forty-five, and honestly, more power to him.
entries.русский: молодец, если так / флаг тебе в руки — одобрение чужого выбора; со скепсисом «дело твоё»
entries.variants: more power to her, more power to 'em
entries.see also: respect, props, go for it

entries.meaning: Praise for something that came out exactly right. Online it is also the standard sarcastic caption for a spectacular failure — a collapsed cake beside the photo it was copied from — so context decides which one is meant.
examples: Nailed it. That presentation could not have gone better.
"How was the audition?" "Nailed it."
You nailed it on the color — that's the exact green she wanted.
He landed the dismount clean and his teammates all yelled "Nailed it!"
The cake collapsed into a puddle of frosting. Nailed it.
entries.русский: в точку! / сделал идеально — разг.; в интернете саркастически о полном провале
entries.variants: you nailed it, crushed it, killed it
entries.see also: boom, way to go, nice one

entries.meaning: Literally praise, but in American speech it is sarcastic more often than not — the thing you say to whoever just knocked the drink over. Said warmly, with the stress falling on nice, it is genuine; said flat, it is a complaint.
examples: Nice going! That's three strikeouts in a row for our guy.
Nice going — now we have to start the whole thing over.
"I locked the keys in the car." "Nice going."
She fixed the leak herself in under an hour. Nice going, honestly.
Real nice going, buddy. The neighbors definitely heard that.
entries.русский: молодец — разг., но чаще саркастически: «ну ты и удружил»
entries.see also: nice one, way to go, good job

entries.meaning: Quick praise for one specific thing — a shot, a joke, a catch, a save. It compliments the act rather than the person, which makes it lighter and easier to say than good job. Like nice going, it flips sarcastic when the "one" was a mistake.
examples: Nice one! That pass was perfect.
She told the joke, and from the back somebody said "nice one."
Nice one on the parking spot — I've circled this block twice already.
You caught the typo in the headline? Nice one.
He spilled coffee down his own shirt. "Nice one," his brother said.
entries.русский: отлично! / хорош! — похвала за одно конкретное действие; легко переходит в сарказм
entries.see also: nice going, nice work, way to go

entries.meaning: The American workplace default for praise between adults — warmer than a nod, less parental than good job, and safe in either direction between a junior and a senior person. It compliments the output rather than the effort.
examples: Nice work on the quarterly numbers.
Nice work, both of you. That was not an easy client.
She read it twice and wrote back two words: "Nice work."
Nice work getting the permit through in a week.
"Nice work out there today," the foreman said, handing back the clipboard.
entries.русский: отличная работа — нейтральная похвала между взрослыми, рабочий стандарт
entries.see also: good job, well done, kudos

entries.meaning: Approval of a suggestion that has finally gotten good. It rewards a change of direction — the first three ideas were fine, this one is right — and now we're talking says the same thing about a situation improving rather than about a person.
examples: "What if we just rent a van and all drive out together?" "Now you're talking."
There's brisket? Now we're talking.
Now you're talking — that's the version I would actually pay for.
He turned the heat up and the onions finally started to color. Now we're talking.
"I could do Friday instead." "Now you're talkin'."
entries.русский: вот это другой разговор! — одобрение наконец удачного предложения
entries.variants: now we're talking, now you're talkin'
entries.see also: that's the spirit, there you go, boom

entries.meaning: Short for proper respect, out of hip-hop and now general American slang. You give props: publicly acknowledging that somebody did something worth acknowledging, often something the speaker could not have pulled off.
examples: Props to Dani for driving all night to get here.
Honestly, props — I would have quit in week two.
Mad props to the kitchen for keeping up with that rush.
He gave her props in front of the whole class, which she did not expect.
Props where props are due: the idea was Marcus's.
entries.русский: респект / уважуха — очень разг., публичное признание заслуг
entries.see also: respect, kudos, hats off

entries.meaning: A one-word salute: what you did was admirable and I acknowledge it. Said alone, usually with a nod, it carries more weight than a longer compliment, because it costs the speaker something to concede.
examples: You walked away from a job that was making you miserable? Respect.
Respect to everybody who showed up in that rain.
He finished the marathon at fifty-eight. Big respect.
"I told my boss exactly what I thought." "Respect."
Respect to the overnight crew — they cleared the whole lot before six.
entries.русский: респект / уважаю — очень разг., односложный салют за поступок
entries.variants: respect to —, big respect, nothing but respect
entries.see also: props, kudos, hats off

entries.meaning: An instruction to accept the credit you have earned, borrowed from the stage; the vowel is the one in now, not the one in low. It is what you say to somebody who is deflecting praise, and to a whole group whose work went well.
examples: Take a bow, chef — that was extraordinary.
Whoever wrote that headline, take a bow.
Take a bow, everybody. Sold out three nights running.
"It was a team thing." "No, this one was you. Take a bow."
The lights came up and the director yelled, "Take a bow!"
entries.русский: поклонись / прими заслуженное — тому, кто отнекивается от похвалы
entries.see also: bravo, hats off, encore

entries.meaning: Approval of an attitude rather than a result. You say it when somebody who was reluctant, discouraged, or grumbling suddenly shows a little willingness — which is also why it works as gentle mockery of forced cheer.
examples: "Fine, I'll try one more time." "That's the spirit."
That's the spirit! Get back on the horse.
She showed up in the rain with a shovel, and her neighbor said, "That's the spirit."
"I'm going to lose, but I'm going to lose loudly." "That's the spirit, I guess."
That's the spirit — now go find out what they'll actually pay.
entries.русский: вот это настрой! — одобрение готовности, а не результата
entries.see also: now you're talking, chin up, keep it up

entries.meaning: Praise for somebody who has just gotten it right after struggling — the verbal pat on the back a parent gives a kid learning to ride a bike. It also means here is the thing you asked for when you hand something over, and see, that's exactly my point in an argument, so tone does the sorting.
examples: There you go! You've got the rhythm now.
There we go — third try and the engine caught.
"There ya go," the barista said, sliding the cup across the counter.
He tied the knot on the first attempt and his grandfather said, "There you go."
"So it was broken the entire time." "There you go."
entries.русский: ну вот! / вот так-то — наконец получилось; также «держи» и «вот именно»
entries.variants: there ya go, there we go, there you go now
entries.see also: now you're talking, attaboy, keep going

entries.meaning: Enthusiastic praise for something somebody just did, standard from the sidelines and the bleachers. The pattern extends freely — way to hustle, way to hang in there — and, like nice going, the flat sarcastic version is common enough that intonation decides the meaning.
examples: Way to go! Two goals in one half.
Way to go, honey — straight A's again.
"Way to hustle out there," the coach said, slapping his shoulder pad.
She got the grant on the first application. Way to go.
Way to go, genius. You just locked us out of the house.
entries.русский: молодец! / так держать — бурная похвала; ровным тоном — сарказм
entries.variants: way to be, way to hustle, way to go!
entries.see also: good job, attaboy, nice going

entries.meaning: Complete, slightly formal praise for a finished piece of work. It is the phrase for writing — a note at the top of a paper, a line in a review — and in American speech it can sound stiff or faintly British next to nice work. The steak sense is unrelated.
examples: Well done. That report answered every question the board had.
"Well done, everyone," she wrote at the top of the memo.
He shook each of their hands and said, "Well done."
Well done on the fundraiser — you beat last year by half.
Very well done — I'd frame this if I were you.
entries.русский: отлично / прекрасная работа — сдержанная похвала, чаще письменная
entries.variants: very well done, well done, you (British)
entries.see also: nice work, good job, bravo

entries.meaning: Encouragement to keep your composure through disappointment, from the posture of not looking down. It is kind but light: right for a small setback, and capable of sounding dismissive after a real loss.
examples: Chin up — there'll be other auditions.
"Keep your chin up," his mother said. "This part doesn't last forever."
Chin up, buttercup. Two more days until Friday.
She patted his arm and told him to keep his chin up.
Chin up. You did everything you could have done.
entries.русский: выше нос! — поддержка при небольшой неудаче
entries.variants: keep your chin up, chin up, buttercup
entries.see also: hang in there, keep going, that's the spirit

entries.meaning: The standard American don't quit for somebody in the middle of something hard and long — an illness, a bad stretch at work, a slow recovery. It promises nothing except that you are watching and you think they can outlast it.
examples: Hang in there — only three more weeks of this schedule.
"Hang in there," the nurse said. "The medication takes a few days to work."
He's been out of work since March, but he's hanging in there.
Hang in there, kiddo. Finals are almost over.
She sent a card with a cat dangling from a branch and "Hang in there" underneath.
entries.русский: держись! / не сдавайся — тому, кто в затяжной трудной полосе
entries.see also: chin up, keep going, you got this

entries.meaning: Straightforward: do not stop now. It is what you say to a runner with a hill left, to a writer in the middle of a draft, and to anybody who has paused to check whether they should keep talking.
examples: Keep going — you're closer than you think.
"Am I boring you?" "No, keep going."
Keep going, three more reps.
He wanted to quit at mile nineteen and somebody on the curb yelled, "Keep going!"
Keep at it. The first fifty pages are always the worst.
entries.русский: продолжай / не останавливайся — ещё немного, не бросай
entries.see also: keep it up, hang in there, go on

entries.meaning: Praise and instruction at once: what you are doing is working, so do more of it. It requires an established pattern — you cannot say it about a one-time success — and it is standard in performance reviews and report-card comments.
examples: Grades are up across the board. Keep it up.
"Keep up the good work," the note on her essay said.
Three straight months under budget — keep it up.
He's been running every morning since January. Keep it up, man.
Keep it going, folks, we're almost through the list.
entries.русский: так держать! — похвала за устойчивый результат: продолжай в том же духе
entries.variants: keep up the good work, keep it going
entries.see also: keep going, good job, nice work

entries.meaning: A flat statement of belief used as a push. It is aimed at somebody who doubts their own ability rather than somebody who is merely tired, and it is one of the few encouragements that works equally well shouted from a sideline and said quietly in a hallway.
examples: You can do it — you've done harder things than this.
"I don't think I can." "You can do this. I've watched you all season."
You can do it, sweetheart. Just let go of the wall.
The whole crowd was chanting "You can do it!" as she came around the last turn.
He looked at the stack of boxes, and his roommate said, "You can do it, one trip at a time."
entries.русский: ты сможешь / у тебя получится — тому, кто сомневается в своих силах
entries.variants: you can do this, I know you can do it
entries.see also: you got this, keep going, go for it

entries.meaning: The modern American confidence-booster, said right before somebody does the hard thing. It is shorter and less earnest than you can do it — the missing have is casual on purpose — and it works in a text as well as it works out loud.
examples: Deep breath. You got this.
She texted "you got this" four minutes before his interview.
You've got this — you wrote the thing, you know it better than anyone in that room.
"You got this, Coach," the assistant said as the timeout ended.
You got this, I promise. Nobody out there is paying as much attention as you think.
entries.русский: ты справишься! / всё получится — разг., короче и легче, чем you can do it
entries.variants: you've got this, you got this, girl
entries.see also: you can do it, go get 'em, break a leg

entries.meaning: The theater's way of wishing good luck without saying the words, since saying them is supposed to jinx the show. It belongs to performers first — actors, musicians, dancers — but it has spread to auditions, interviews, and anything with a nervous person walking into a room.
examples: Break a leg out there tonight.
"Break a leg," the stage manager whispered as the curtain went up.
She has her recital at four, so text her break a leg.
Break a leg at the interview. Call me the second you're out.
He hates being told good luck, so we all just say break a leg.
entries.русский: ни пуха ни пера! — театральное пожелание удачи вместо запретного «удачи»
entries.see also: knock 'em dead, good luck, go get 'em

entries.meaning: Hope rather than confidence, from the superstitious gesture. It is used about outcomes nobody in the conversation controls — a test result, a verdict, a flight in bad weather — and it works both as a wish for somebody else and as an admission of your own nerves.
examples: Fingers crossed the inspection goes clean tomorrow.
"Any word from the hospital?" "Not yet. Fingers crossed."
We're on standby for the six a.m. — fingers crossed.
Fingers crossed for you both. I know how much you want this house.
She said "fingers crossed" and actually held them up.
entries.русский: скрестим пальцы / тьфу-тьфу-тьфу — надежда на то, что от нас не зависит
entries.variants: keeping my fingers crossed, fingers and toes crossed
entries.see also: good luck, break a leg, knock 'em dead

entries.meaning: A send-off that tells somebody to fight hard and not be polite about it. It carries a faint political echo from Harry Truman's 1948 campaign, and it fits arguments, elections, games, and hearings — anywhere the other side has it coming.
examples: Give 'em hell in there. Don't let them talk over you.
"Give 'em hell, Harry!" somebody shouted from the back of the crowd.
She's testifying Thursday. Give 'em hell.
Give 'em heck, kiddo — it's only a spelling bee.
He shook my hand at the door and said, "Give 'em hell."
entries.русский: задай им жару! / всыпь им — напутствие драться и не церемониться
entries.see also: knock 'em dead, go get 'em, sic 'em

entries.meaning: The universal send-off before something uncertain, safe in every register from a text to a formal letter. Said with a particular flatness it curdles: good luck with that means you're going to need it, and I'm not helping.
examples: Good luck on the exam tomorrow.
"Best of luck in your new role," the card read.
Good luck — I'll be thinking about you all afternoon.
He wished her good luck and meant it, which surprised them both.
"I'm going to ask him to lower the rent." "Good luck with that."
entries.русский: удачи! — универсальное напутствие; ровным тоном — «ну-ну, удачи тебе»
entries.variants: best of luck, good luck to you, lots of luck (usually sarcastic)
entries.see also: break a leg, fingers crossed, godspeed

entries.meaning: A send-off with swagger: go impress them so thoroughly that they do not recover. It suits performances, presentations, and interviews, and it assumes an audience — you cannot knock 'em dead alone in a room.
examples: Knock 'em dead tonight. I want to hear all about it.
"You look great. Now go knock 'em dead."
She's got the pitch at nine — knock 'em dead, kid.
Knock 'em dead, and don't forget to breathe between slides.
He straightened his son's collar and said, "Knock 'em dead."
entries.русский: порви их! / срази наповал — напутствие перед выступлением или собеседованием
entries.variants: knock them dead, knock 'em out, go knock 'em dead
entries.see also: break a leg, go get 'em, good luck
